doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
title: Recording 'That's The Way It Goes' and Goodman's silent reaction
summary: The 1984 record's personnel and RCA session, and Goodman playing it in the background without comment; chauffeuring him.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Later on, as the band got professional and as I started to make a living in music, all those guys, I mean I paid. I paid for arrangements. I paid arrangers and I paid — but at this time there was nothing there. So John Hammond and a few other things and things started, and next thing you know we’re going to make a record. So we made a record for a guy named Jerry Valburn who issued a lot of radio broadcasts with like a big jazz collector who had his own little labels. And he had a label and he started recording and stuff, so I was going to make a big band record for him, if I could pay for the band and he would put it out. So we did a record, it was called “That’s The Way It Goes” in 1984, and the band on that record was Dick Katz, Howard Alden, Phil Flanigan, Mel Lewis, Bobby Pring, Eddie Bert and Matt Finders, or maybe Bobby Pring missed as he was on tour with the Widespread Depression band, and my sax section was already set — it was set for a while. Chuck Wilson and Jack Stooky on altos, Ken Peplowski and Doug Lawrence on tenors, and Danny Bank. And the trumpets were, on that first album, Paulie Cohen, Laurie Frink, Dick Sudhalter and John Eckert. And so that was the band. We made this record. It was pretty damn good. We did it at the old RCA studios. I mean it was the old RCA studios on tape with a legendary engineer named Bob Simpson. And it was really, really great. So we made the record and I gave a copy to Goodman, who I was working for still at that time. And I said, “Here’s my record.” Because we recorded a few of his things. He never said a word about it. Man, he never said like it’s good, it’s bad. And I’m 25 years old or whatever, I’m dying for him to say something. You know, tell me something. And then the way it worked was Goodman’s office, his office and his apartment were in a building called the Manhattan House which is on East 66th Street between Second and Third Avenues. He had the penthouse on Third Avenue, and on the Second Avenue side of the building was a little one bedroom apartment that was his office. So I would go to work in the office, he’d be up in his penthouse on the other avenue over here, and he would call and say, you know, bring the checks up or I’m meeting someone for lunch, or can you come up and have lunch there’s nobody, you know. And so we kind of went back and forth. He started calling me from his apartment with my record playing in the background, but he didn’t say anything. You know. I don’t know if that’s what you call passive-aggressive or I don’t know what the word is but he was messing with me. And I’d hear my record in the background. And of course I’m dying to say well, well, but I wouldn’t, I wouldn’t give in you know. Well finally one day, I mean this anecdote sounds improbable, and it is improbable. He lived in Stamford, Connecticut on Rock Rimmon Road. And his girlfriend at that time, his wife had died, his girlfriend was a woman named Carol Phillips, who ran Clinique, which is a woman’s make-up like stuff you know? And you know, make-up and perfume and hand cream and eyelash stuff and all that kind — a boutique thing. And they were going out together. And
